title: When Scope Changes, Ask What Moves Out
summary: New work will land mid-sprint. Make the plan visible, ask what moves out, hammer the request down and name the trade-off out loud so nobody absorbs it in silence.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The request lands right after lunch, in that careful tone people use when they know the plan is already full. A customer needs one more report. Sales wants "just a small export." Support found a case where the new checkout flow gets awkward. Nobody is trying to cause chaos. There isn't a single empty slot left on the board.

Most teams handle this moment in one of two bad ways. Either they say yes to everything and pay for it later in overtime and skipped tests, or someone says "no" and it lands as attitude. There's a better middle path, and it mostly comes down to one question.

Scope changes are normal

A changing plan doesn't automatically mean someone planned badly. The Agile Manifesto says it outright: "Welcome changing requirements, even late in development" (Principles behind the Agile Manifesto). A regulation changes. A customer finally describes the need properly. Discovery turns up a technical limit. A competitor ships something. A plan is the best guess you could make with what you knew at the time, and better information should be allowed to change it.

Ryan Singer puts it more bluntly in Shape Up, Chapter 14, "Decide When to Stop": "Scope grows naturally. Scope creep isn't the fault of bad clients, bad managers, or bad programmers" (Shape Up). You can't see all the small details of a project until you're inside the work. So the goal isn't to stop scope from growing. It's to get good at deciding, again and again, what stays.

The trouble is additions with no trade-off

Things go wrong when a change is treated as pure addition. One more field, one more screen, one more report, one more integration. Each sounds small on its own. Stacked up, they eat testing time, design attention, review capacity and the team's confidence on release day. Nobody decided to cut those. They disappeared.

So before debating the request, put the current plan where everyone can see it. What's already committed? What's in progress? Which decisions are still open? Which parts are risky because they touch production behavior, a data migration or a team outside yours? With the plan on the table, people argue about the plan instead of trading gut feelings.

Ask what moves out

"Can we do this?" is the wrong question. Given enough time, a team can do almost anything. The useful one is: if this comes in, what moves out or moves later?

Scrum has a guard rail for this inside a sprint. The Scrum Guide says that during the Sprint "no changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal," "quality does not decrease," and "scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned." Two things follow from that. Renegotiation is expected and it goes through the PO, so it doesn't happen in a DM to one developer. And "we'll skip the tests this once" is off the table: quality isn't one of the things you trade. (Your team's Definition of Done is where that bar is written down.)

That leaves a short menu:

OptionWhen it fitsWhat to say
SwapThe new work matters more than something not yet started"We can take this if the CSV export moves to next sprint."
ShrinkThe need is real but the first version can be smaller"We can ship the report with three filters now, the rest after."
DeferIt's useful but not urgent"Let's put it at the top of the next planning."
Move the date, openlyEverything in the plan really has to ship together"If all of it stays, release moves from the 12th to the 19th."
DeclineIt doesn't serve the goal you're working toward"It doesn't fit this goal. Here's why, and here's who to ask."

Notice what's missing: "fine, we'll absorb it." That's the option that turns into overtime, skipped reviews and a release nobody trusts.

Shrink the request before you weigh it

Basecamp calls this scope hammering, "forcefully questioning a design, implementation, or use case to cut scope and finish inside the fixed time box" (Shape Up). The questions from that chapter work well on any incoming request:

  • Is this a must-have? Could we ship without it?
  • Is this a new problem, or one customers already live with today?
  • How likely is this case, and which customers see it when it happens?
  • Is it core, used by everyone, or more of an edge case?

The same chapter suggests comparing down to baseline instead of up to an ideal: how do customers handle this today, without the feature? A request often shrinks a lot once you ask that. Maybe the "small export" is really "finance needs last month's numbers once, by Friday," and someone can run a query.

How you say it matters

A bare "no" sounds personal when the team has no shared picture of the trade-offs. "We can include this if we move that report to next week" gives the conversation a shape. It takes the request seriously without pretending capacity is infinite, and it puts the cost in front of the people who get to choose.

Everyone brings a different piece of the cost. Engineering brings what it'll really take, without turning that into a wall. Product brings the user and business context, without reading delivery limits as resistance. Design, QA and support each see costs the others miss. A good scope conversation gets all of that on the table before the plan turns into pressure.

Some changes should be accepted in five minutes. Some should be split. Some should be declined. Handling scope well can still be fast. What matters is naming the consequence before the team absorbs it without a word. A hidden cost turns into resentment over a few sprints. A named cost is a decision, and it's worth writing down in your decision log so nobody has to reconstruct it later.

Try this week

  • Next time a request lands mid-sprint, reply with "what should move out to make room?" before you estimate anything.
  • Run the request through the four hammering questions and see how much of it survives.
  • Write down one trade-off your team made silently last sprint, and say it out loud at the retro.
  • Agree with your PO that sprint scope changes go through them, so nobody negotiates in a side DM.

Scope will keep changing. Real work always turns up things the plan couldn't see. Next time a request lands mid-sprint, open the board first, point at the card that would have to move, and let the PO make the call.

faqs.q: Is scope change a sign of bad planning?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. The Agile Manifesto asks teams to welcome changing requirements, even late in development, and Shape Up notes that scope grows naturally because you can't see every detail until you're inside the work. The problem is adding work without deciding what moves out.

faqs.q: What should you ask when a new request lands mid-sprint?
faqs.a: Ask what moves out or moves later if this comes in. Then pick from a short menu: swap it with work not yet started, shrink the first version, defer it, move the date openly, or decline it with a reason. Absorbing it silently is the option to avoid.

faqs.q: Can scope change during a Scrum sprint?
faqs.a: Yes, within limits. The Scrum Guide says no changes should endanger the Sprint Goal, quality does not decrease, and scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned. So changes go through the Product Owner and never come out of quality.

A term from Basecamp's Shape Up: forcefully questioning a design, implementation or use case to cut scope so the work fits a fixed time box. Typical questions are whether something is a must-have, whether customers already live with the problem, how likely the case is and who it affects.

faqs.q: How do you say no to a scope change without sounding difficult?
faqs.a: Offer a trade-off instead of a bare no, for example: we can include this if the report moves to next week. It respects the request, shows the cost and lets the person with the authority make the call.
